Geography

Litland is a duchy in the south of Polaris, it is also called Little Earth. According to the Polari Land Guide, it stretches along the east coast of the mainland south of Mason Bay and borders Hope, Shepherd's Meadows and Shimmery. The name is short for "small land", although in fact Litland is comparable in area to Almera or Darquater: the first settlers considered only a strip of meadows in the Holliwell floodplain suitable for life. (Duchy of Almera; Darkwater) Most of the duchy is jungle-covered plains; the climate is tropical and humid. The Earth is permeated by the huge Holliwell Delta, and monsoons from the Sunny Ocean bring pronounced seasons of rain. Mechanic Louis, who built a rail track here, found that the Litland winter is not so warm: there is no snow, but every other day there are cold showers.

To the west, the duchy is separated from Reis County by the Holy River Holliwell. (Hollywell) Along its lower course lie the Shepherd's Meadow - a huge steppe, which by the law of Juliana the Great is considered a common possession of six neighboring lands. On the four lower fords are the fortresses of Litland; Rebecca Litland grew up in such a fortress among the Shepherd Meadows and recalled that from the top of the tower, only the “green ocean” of grass is visible to the south, west and north. In the Halliwell Delta is the town of Surlion, "one foot in Litland, the other in the Shimmery Kingdom."

Jungles are called "rope forests"; the Litlanders consider them sacred, "good to their own and impassable to strangers." The border between the forest and the steppe is very sharp: the road to Melorange goes along the riverbed of the Orange River, dried up in time immemorial, and rope forests stand on its left hand, and meadows on the right. There are huge spiders in the jungle - everyone loves them, as one northerner complained, in Bassifor.

Cities

  • Melorange is the duchy's two hundred thousandth capital: white sandstone houses, rooftop flower beds, palm alleys, magnolia gardens, three stationary theaters, and street actors in a dozen squares. The Lithuanians are so famous for their health that there were only three hospitals in the city, and in 1774 the wounded had to be placed in the homes of the citizens.
  • Bassifor is the ancestral castle of the dukes near Melorange; Becca compared the uncle-duke to the spider in the center of the network, and the father-Lord of the Chamber called the “string of the uncle’s web”, stretching to the capital. In the castle there is a huge library, allegedly the best in the South.
  • The Rain Forest is a port on the coast, about sixty miles northeast of Melorange, sheltered by a patch of jungle; Prince Hector's fleet was to arrive there in January 1775.
  • Colmin is a port on the coast; in 1775, Count Vittor's men took seventy ships from Leixity to Colmin to delay the crossing of Erwin's army.
  • Maple is a port forty miles from Melorange, to which a road through the steppe leads from the capital. In 1774, the Shavans burned it to the ground, and Adrian's army saw in its place "a bald spot among the meadows"; in the summer of 1775, the port of Maple again received ships - the Sea Arrow and the ships of the Volta stood here.
  • The shallow water is named in the conversation of the Shavans (at Cort) among the large cities of Litland lying in the jungle or on the shore.
  • Melville is a trading town at the fork of the tracks, abandoned by the residents at the approach of the horde.
  • Surlion is a large port in the Holliwell Delta on the border with Shimmery; houses here stand on stilts like doves.

Economy

According to the Traveler, Litland’s economy is “very specific” and depends sharply on trade. The duchy is the main producer of spices, dyes and flavors, and in the depths, at the Shepherd's Meadows, there are famous horse factories; in the novels, the "litland horses" are valued, and Becca rode the "red May-litlanders". Litland is also famous for pepper honey, strong spicy tinctures, silk (Harmon mentioned the "silk famine in Litland") and rubber, from which the rims of the wheels for imperial trains are made.

At the same time, flour, cereals, vegetable oil, weapons, metal and glass products are imported from the outside, the duchy does not have its large shipyards, and the fleets of the Crown, Shimmery and the Southern Way carry out the transportation; they joke that the treasury of Litland is a leaky bucket. There is also no spark here, and the duke receives a spark from the Lands of the Crown. The Duke of Farway's men built a rail road to Litland. After the Lightharts lost the Heart of Light and the East-West trade route disintegrated, the ships of the Crown and the Labelins, going from north to south, began to enter the parking lot in the ports of Litland. (House Lightheart) Nevertheless, ordinary Lithuanians are not poor: the coastal forests are abundant, food is easily obtained, and, according to the Guide, the poor Lithuanian almost every evening dances and sings, while a wealthy peasant of the Southern Way bends his back six days a week.

In 1774, the Ambassadors of Reis proposed to the Litlands that a protected road be built through the Shepherds of the Meadow and Reis to the west coast, so that the Litland spices would go to the North bypassing the Crown and the Southern Way. After the war of 1774–1775, Litland suffered more than other lands, and Lady Minerva halved the duties on Litland goods and arranged a fair of Litland goods on Palace Island.

People and Customs

The Guide calls the Lithuanians perhaps the most cheerful people of the Empire. Everything here is “exaggerated”: giant trees, flowers are too fragrant, fruits are fabulously sweet, shower such that in five seconds you will soak to the thread. Litlanders paint houses with patterns, wear bright clothes and large jewelry, dye their hair in lilac, yellow, raspberry. Their songs are fun and more often convey a mood than a meaning. It is not customary to restrain feelings here: the Lithuanian shouts, laughs, hugs a friend and weeps openly, which makes these feelings seem hypocritical to the northerners. The common people are free in their views of marriage, nudity is not considered shameful; only the lords try to maintain marital fidelity for the sake of clarity of inheritance. These features are most strongly seen in villages among the jungle; in cities and forts near the Shepherd's Meadows, they are smoothed out.

The novels confirm this image. Manson noticed that the inhabitants of Melorange do not hide anything - rejoicing, laughing, sad, crying - and the feast in Bassifor had all the colors of the rainbow and sounded "like a June downpour." Lady Sophia found the Meloranges to be "simple-minded, childlike people" who embrace and kiss in public, but on stage turn out to be great actors. When the wounded died in the houses of the townspeople, the Litlanders wept over them as over their own children.

Litland considers himself the South, and in the eyes of the Empire he is the South along with Shimmery. The Shimmerians regard him as a "younger brother": smaller, more victorious and weaker, but also the South; according to the "Guide", they are sure that the real southerners are only them, and the Litlanders are half-breeds, something between the southerners and Westerners. The Litland captives in Shimmery are regarded as "almost white-blooded".

Ruling House

The Duchy is ruled by the Great House of Lithland of the Yangmei family. (House Litland) In 1774–1775, the duke was Willas, a scribe who rarely leaves Bassifor and loves everything written on paper. Becca compared him to a spider in the middle of the web. His brother Douglas is Rebecca's father, and the Duke's chief advisor and Litland's second representative in the House was Lord Brandon Coss. Willas had four sons, "Lords of the Jungle and the Coast", and Douglas had three daughters. Becca considered herself the "living coat of arms of the Litlands".

History

According to the "Guide", the settlers who came from the north were so afraid of the jungle that they did not settle where they can be seen, considered the forest as a refuge of Ido and called it "where the thick" or "grown ropes". Around the 9th century, the brave, attracted by the sweetness of fruits and freedom from hierarchy, began to settle in the jungle. In the twelfth century, Duchess Paolina Litland recognised the benefits of the spice trade, sent detachments into the jungle, and discovered that it was already full of “cheerful, smiling people”; she assimilated them instead of enslaving them, and the jungle people gave the lords knowledge of spices and dyes, labour, shelter during the dark years of the First Horse War, and their optimism.

In the sixteenth century, the rebel Darian devastated Litland: in Shavan legend, he conquered both the Lesser Land and the Crown’s cities as far as the walls of Faunterra (the Horse Wars). The neighborhood with the nomads of the West is the eternal headache of the duchy: the Shavans drive herds through fords, steal cattle and kill shepherds, the Lithuanians pay the same.

In the Novels

Brody and the fair of brides

In January 1774, Erwin Origin offered the Duke of Willas a deal: the Litlands would take possession of all four fords through Holliwell and be able to decide for themselves who to let on the east bank, and in return would recognize any bride Adrian and support his reforms. This meant abandoning Becky's claim to the crown, and the Litlands agreed. Then in the hands of the Litlends fell a lazy letter to the fords, as if granted by the emperor, and they "on joy" took over the crossings. The Westerners believed that Adrian had violated Julian’s law by giving up common lands to “his henchmen”; Adrian himself was convinced that the letter was fake and planted to provoke war, first he blamed Origin for it, then attributed it to a third force. When, after Evergard, the lord demanded a personal oath from the great lords, the Duke of Litland, referring to the “border conflict” with the Westerners, sent his brother instead. In the summer at Lacy's estate in the Lands of the Crown, Racy's ambassadors, led by Count Damir, proposed an alliance; Lord Coss demanded half of the Shepherd's Meadows, and then negotiations ended in massacre, an ambush in Lacy (August 1774). (Ambush at Lacey)

War with the Horde

The Shavans, led by Moran Steppe Fire, then captured the crossings through Holliwell and invaded Litland. Moran did not spend time storming castles, but rushed east, burning villages and cities, and passed the entire meadow part of the duchy. The knighthood of Litland — about two thousand heavy and four thousand light horsemen, "all that the duke had," gave battle at the edge of the jungle, thirty miles from the capital. The Shavans parted, let the latin cavalry through their ranks, and beat her in the back. The infantry went to the rope forests, where the steppes did not go. According to the Shavans, the horde burned down seven cities; in Maple, Adrian's army found a church littered with mutilated bodies. However, everything that Litland cherished, took refuge in the jungle: the big cities - Maple, Rain Forest, shallow water - lie in the forests or on the shore, and raids on the villages did not lure the enemy from behind the walls.

In December 1774, Emperor Adrian and Prince Hector of Shimmery defeated a horde at Meloranj, after which the Duke staged a three-day feast in Basifor in honor of the generals. In the winter of 1775, Shavan scouts Neymir and Chara made their way across Litland; they saw mourning ribbons in Melorange's windows after Adrian's death, and the horde, contrary to Hector's expectations, turned not to the Rain Forest, but north, to the capital. (Neimir) In the spring of 1775, Moran laid siege to Melorange again. The city was held by the militia and the spark regiment of General William Davey, and then Minerva forced Moran to take her vassal oath and leave for Holliwell, releasing the captured Lithuanians. (William Davy) Davey later resented that the "Voice of the Crown" credited Meloranj Minerva's rescue, although the Shawnees had stormed three times and were repulsed by his regiment and militia. Lady Sophia responded by mimicking the article he would have liked to read: “The valiant General Davy, with a single regiment, soundly defeated a horde forty thousand strong. The Knights of Litland helped him a little - they brought porridge with chops." Minerva, he then threw: “It was the Duke of Litland and I who kept Melorange.” His regiment stood in the only quarter of Melorange not to recognize the power of the dukes.

After the war

According to Becky, the war devastated a third of Litland, and at the court in 1775 it was said that "in Litland it was hungry after the Shavan invasion." At the Marengo House, Lord Litland was outraged when Ganta Thunderstorm offered to recognize the heroes and the Shavans: "You have robbed, burned, raped! Steal our horses and our daughters!" Groza replied that the Litlandes had killed the Shavanese ambassadors and appropriated the crossings; due to the objections of the House of Litland, the vote to approve the actions of Reis, Northwood, and Holliwell was postponed. Minerva later met with an inspection in Litland, and the Lithuanian ambassadors invited her to the sea in the summer. In the summer of 1775 Lady Sophia Origin came to Melorange and Maple; at the port of Maple, she was met by Mireille Nan-Claire with foltian ships. (Mireille Nen-Clair) In Humans and Gods, the deposed Adrian expected to find support in Litland and pass through the Miran Pass to Surlion.

The Author's Article

The author’s article about Litland was published on Fandom in 2021. (Source) Its text coincides with the section of the Guide already recounted above; only a few details about manners were not included in the retelling.

  • Love for everything. Lithuanians are polygamous. In the hinterland there are villages where the entire adult population is actually one family: each child is considered common, and any adult cares for him. The Right Northerner loves the North, the sharp blade and the suzerain, and the Litlander loves everything - kin, althess, friends, village, jungle, monkeys and downpours. Loving one thing, one thing, or one person is like a prison sentence.
  • Misunderstandings with the North. Northern historians, visiting Litland, wrote: “These strange people have fun at the funeral!” In fact, the Litlanders mourn loved ones, but so openly that it seems to the North a clown.
  • Fear of the jungle. The first settlers, speaking of the jungle, superstitiously added "zur-zur" and created a sacred spiral: it was believed that the forest itself could come and eat someone who called him too loudly.

Trivia

  • Becca called the obsession with horses a common trait of the genus: “Each Litland has its own obsession.”
  • Mira in "A Doll on the Throne" compared the prisoner's thick hair to the Litland jungle, and in the ancient Arden in the Crownlands, among ostriches, lemurs and macaques under the feet of passers-by, "the furry Litland pigs" were grunted.
  • The Litland lordchild, who had killed an assistant postal manager in a duel, was caught by Mark's men and put on trial.
  • Among the items that changed owners for obvious reasons is the Third Bird, donated by Duke Farway to Duke Litland.
  • In Fantasia, Infanta Demeter observes that the smell of mango and orange "conjures thoughts of Litland, and Litland has long been unheard of." In "Fantasies" "Ad-ri-an!" (Election of the sovereign, 1776) Duke Litland is listed among Adrian’s clear supporters, and Francis-Ilian allows that Litland may leave the Empire after Minerva’s accession.
